accuracy.evidence: Path of light (source to object to eye, never eye outwards) matches NC England Y6 Light ('we see things because light travels from light sources to our eyes or from light sources to objects and then to our eyes'). Parts and jobs (pupil a hole in the iris, lens focuses onto the retina, retina sends signals along the optic nerve, brain interprets) match BBC Bitesize KS2 'How do we see?' and the topic evidence. Lens shape checked: thinner for far objects, fatter for near (accommodation), and the retinal image is inverted. Pupil sizes in items (2-4 mm in bright light, up to 7-8 mm in the dark) sit inside the normal adult range; every parameter corner gives 2-7 mm.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented 'eyes send out rays' idea (Driver et al. 1985; Osborne et al. 1990 SPACE report on light): the first prediction, the eye-first tap feedback and challenge tag 'out'. Also the pupil as a painted dot (parts predict, m1, tag 'dot'), the pupil shrinking in the dark (pupil predict, size feedback, m2, tag 'size'), the picture forming on the lens or pupil (focus feedback, p4, tag 'lens') and the eye rather than the brain doing the seeing (chain predict and order feedback, m6, tag 'brain').

lab_distinct.evidence: flageye is built on the eye's own mechanism: a light path that must run lamp, ball, eye (and lamp, eye for a light source), a side section of the eye with leader-line labels for iris, pupil, lens, retina and optic nerve, front views with three pupil sizes matched to the light in a place, a lens whose thickness moves the point where rays meet in front of, on or behind the retina, and the five-step chain to the brain. None of it works for another topic by swapping labels.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers each idea before the text states it: starting the path at the eye is refused, so light has to start at the source; rays visibly cross in front of the retina with a fat lens for the far tree and land behind it with a thin lens for the near book, and only on the retina does a sharp upside-down picture appear; the order cards will not accept the brain before the optic nerve. Done messages confirm the rule after the task is finished.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: light 'from my eye out to the ball' (the path refuses the eye as a start), pupil as 'a black dot painted on the eye' (it is labelled as the gap in the iris), pupil 'gets smaller' in the dark (the dark bedroom only accepts the big pupil), the retinal picture 'the right way up' (the sharp image is drawn inverted) and 'the eye' works out what we see (the chain ends at the brain).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; wrong options are tagged to seven distinct messages: out (eyes take light in), source (a book is lit, it does not glow), dot (the pupil is a hole and looks black because light does not come back out), size (bigger in the dark), lens (the lens bends, the retina catches the picture), brain (the brain interprets) and iris (the coloured ring). Answer order rotates every question.

readability.evidence: Kid text is short sentences with one idea each and the precise curriculum terms (pupil, iris, lens, retina, optic nerve) introduced with what they do; FK grade 1.6 for kid and 8.0 for adult, inside the family limits (5.0 and 10.0). Canvas prompts give one action each, such as 'Make the far tree sharp on the retina'.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: how light reaches the eye, the pupil as a hole, the lens and the upside-down picture, the optic nerve and brain, pupil size. Adult paragraphs: curriculum placement and key words, a torch activity, five named mistakes, what each scene does. The content gate's filler list and 12% overlap check pass, and nothing repeats the light-in-straight-lines lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px screenshots in light and dark: the five label slots sit two to the left and right of a 72 px eye with leader lines, name cards are in rows of 3 and 2 about 100 px wide and 34 px tall, the three pupil cards are 105 px squares, the focus scene shows the far tree, rays and retina with the 'sharp, upside down' note centred under the eye, and the order step sizes its 10 rows to fit the canvas height. The iPhone 13 walkthrough completes every Show me.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Light goes to the lamp/ball/eye', 'Pick Iris' then 'Put it on the label at the top left' (and the other four positions), a pupil size button per place, 'Make the lens thinner', 'Make the lens fatter' and 'It is sharp', and one button per step card. The canvas aria-label reports every result; axe WCAG 2.1 AA runs clean in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
